ring:U1.what: The main chip. It runs the ring's program, handles Bluetooth and USB, and receives the microphone signals.
ring:U1.why: It is the brain of the ring: every other part is set up and read by this chip.

ring:U2.what: The power chip. It charges the cell and makes the steady supply voltages the other parts need.
ring:U2.why: The cell's voltage is not what the chips need, so this chip charges it safely and shares the power out.

ring:R71.what: A small resistor that tells the power chip which output voltage to give.
ring:R71.why: The power chip reads this resistor at start-up, so the main chip gets the right voltage.

ring:R72.what: A small resistor that tells the power chip which output voltage to give.
ring:R72.why: The power chip reads this resistor at start-up, so the main chip gets the right voltage.

ring:R73.what: A resistor from the charging line to ground. It empties the charging line when the ring leaves its case.
ring:R73.why: Without it the charging pad on your finger would keep several volts for a while after the ring leaves the case.

ring:U3.what: The storage chip. It holds the recorded audio inside the ring.
ring:U3.why: The ring records on its own, so the audio waits here until it is copied off.

ring:U10.what: A small chip that translates the signals between the main chip and the storage chip.
ring:U10.why: The main chip talks at 1.8 volts and the storage chip at 3.0 volts; without it they cannot understand each other.

ring:U4.what: The screen supply chip. It turns the cell's voltage into the two voltages the screen needs.
ring:U4.why: The screen needs a higher voltage and a negative voltage that the cell cannot give directly.

ring:U5.what: A microphone. It hears sound through a small hole in the underside of the block.
ring:U5.why: Two microphones together give a stereo recording of the voices around the wearer.

ring:U6.what: A microphone. It hears sound through a small hole in the underside of the block.
ring:U6.why: Two microphones together give a stereo recording of the voices around the wearer.

ring:DISP1.what: The screen, a small display set under the cover glass on top of the block.
ring:DISP1.why: It shows the wearer what the ring is doing, and the joystick moves around on it.

ring:J1.what: A tiny connector on the main board that the screen's flat cable plugs into.
ring:J1.why: It joins the screen to the main board so the chip can send pictures to the screen.

ring:ANT1.what: The antenna. It sends and receives the Bluetooth radio signal.
ring:ANT1.why: Without it the ring cannot talk to a phone.

ring:L2.what: A small part of the antenna matching set. Together they tune the radio signal between chip and antenna.
ring:L2.why: Tuning the match lets the radio signal pass cleanly instead of being reflected back. One position is left empty for later tuning.

ring:X1.why: The chip needs a steady clock for the radio and for keeping time, and a crystal keeps it exact.

ring:X2.what: A crystal. It makes a very steady beat that the main chip uses as its clock.

ring:FB1.what: A filter bead on the chip's supply line. It blocks electrical noise.
ring:FB1.why: Noise on the supply would disturb the radio, so this bead keeps it clean.

ring:M1.what: The vibration motor in the band, on the joystick side.
ring:M1.why: It buzzes to confirm start, stop and warnings when you cannot look at the screen.

ring:U11.what: The motor's own supply chip. It feeds the vibration motor straight from the cell.
ring:U11.why: The motor's start current is higher than the power chip allows, so the motor gets its own supply.

ring:C83.what: A capacitor beside the motor's supply chip. It is a small local energy store.
ring:C83.why: It keeps the motor's supply steady at the moment the motor starts.

ring:C84.what: The capacitor at the output of the motor's supply chip.
ring:C84.why: It holds the motor's supply steady. It was made smaller so that a motor start no longer pulls the cell voltage too low.

ring:BT1.what: Battery cell, curved to follow the inside of the band. It stores the energy that runs the ring.
ring:BT1.why: It is thin and long, so it fits the band instead of the block, which keeps the block flat.

ring:PRT1.what: The protection circuit of the cell, on the cell's tab.
ring:PRT1.why: It cuts the cell off if it is overcharged or shorted, so the ring stays safe.

ring:PCB1.what: The main circuit board. The chips and small parts sit on it and are wired together.
ring:PCB1.why: It holds everything electronic in one flat piece, inside the block under the screen.

ring:ADH1.what: A clear adhesive layer between the glass and the screen.
ring:ADH1.why: It glues the glass to the screen and leaves no air gap that would blur the picture.

ring:SEAL1.what: A thin seal ring between the cover glass and the metal body.
ring:SEAL1.why: It keeps water and dust from getting in around the edge of the glass.

ring:DAM1.what: A small frame of cured glue around the joystick's switches.

case:U1.what: The case's main chip, a small computer on a module.
case:U1.why: It runs the case: it reads the ring, drives the light and uploads recordings.

case:U2.what: The case's charger chip. It charges the case cell and powers the ring.
case:U2.why: It lets one USB-C cable charge the case and, through the case, the ring.

case:U3.what: A voltage regulator that makes a steady supply for the case chips.
case:U3.why: The chips need a steady voltage, and the cell's voltage changes as it empties.

case:U4.what: A memory chip in the case. It holds recordings copied from the ring.
case:U4.why: It keeps the audio safe until the case sends it on.

case:U5.what: A switch with a current limit for the ring's charging line.
case:U5.why: It protects the case and the ring if something shorts the charging pins.

case:L1.what: A coil in the case's charging circuit.
case:L1.why: The charger chip needs it to turn the supply into the charging current.

case:L2.what: A coil in the case's voltage regulator.
case:L2.why: The regulator needs it to produce a steady supply.

case:J1.what: The USB-C socket of the case.
case:J1.why: You plug the charging cable in here.

case:LED1.why: It shows the owner the state of the case and the ring.

case:BT1.why: It stores the energy that charges the ring away from a wall socket.

case:PCB1.why: It carries the case chips and joins them together.

case:PCB2.what: A small circuit board that carries the four contact pins.
case:PCB2.why: It brings the ring's charging contacts out to the main board.

case:MECH1.what: The case shell, a soft pebble shape.
case:MECH1.why: It holds the parts and gives the ring its seat.

case:MECH2.what: The case lid, a crowned cap that swivels aside.
case:MECH2.why: It closes the case and covers the ring.

case:MECH3.what: The bottom plate that closes the underside of the case.
case:MECH3.why: It holds the case parts in place from below.

case:MECH4.what: A hidden metal pin that the lid turns around.

case:MECH5.what: The centre post that the ring lies around.
case:MECH5.why: It holds the pin board and the four pins against the pads on the inside of the band.

case:MECH8.what: A thin glide disc between the lid and the shell.
case:MECH8.why: It lets the lid swivel smoothly and without scratching.

case:MECH9.what: A small magnet, one in the shell and one in the lid.
case:MECH9.why: The pair holds the lid closed.

case:MECH7.what: A clear fill in the window of the case light.
case:MECH7.why: It lets the light show through and seals the opening.

case:P1-P4.what: A spring-loaded contact pin that touches one pad of the ring.
case:P1-P4.why: It carries charging power and data between the case and the ring.
